Lessons.Title: Non-unit Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Original warm-up shows four whole squares each divided into FOUR equal regions: 1 part shaded (1/4),2 shaded (2/4),3 shaded (3/4),4 shaded (4/4). The original third figure is explicitly labelled3/4. Emphasize more than ONE shaded part may be represented as a fraction.

Activity1 Write and Read Fractions contains TWO ORIGINAL TABLE GRAPHICS, both read from the owner-device source, not inferred from alt text. TABLE1 source five rows:1/4 (one fourth),3/4 (three fourths),4/4 (four fourths),2/3 (two thirds),3/8 (three eighths). TABLE2 three rows:4/6 (four sixths),6/4 (six fourths),7/6 (seven sixths). For every row identify count shaded, size1/denominator, word name, written fraction.

Crucial improper case:6/4 uses TWO separate quartered whole rectangles, first4/4 shaded and second2/4 shaded, giving6 fourths. Likewise7/6 uses two rectangles, one fully shaded6/6 plus1/6 shaded on next, giving7 sixths. Both are greater than one whole and source-equivalent model must reflect two wholes.

Activity2 Fraction Match uses a first publisher game deck (blackline master), one round of memory matching diagrams with number fractions, then Part2's EIGHT blank cards to produce FOUR NEW diagram/number pairs, followed by a second round using all pairs. Original rules: all face-down, flip two cards, keep matched cards and play again; no more than two matches in a turn. Human evaluation of created cards and partner explanations.

Original lesson activity synthesis notes2/2,3/3,4/4,6/6 all equivalent to1 whole. Synthesis contrasts unit fraction1/8 and non-unit5/8; and example7/6 as one full sixths rectangle plus one sixth. The original teacher edition deliberately postpones formal terms NUMERATOR/DENOMINATOR until later, so describe 'top number' and 'bottom number' without introducing named terms as if taught here.

All five original illustrative assets including two multirow table graphics visually inspected; newly drawn Edulytics equivalents only. Publisher physical blackline decks, full student task PDF and gated Shaded Fraction Cool-down are not certified, tests/Stage D not run.

KeyConcepts.Title: Count unit fractions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A non-unit fraction a/b consists of a pieces each of size1/b of one whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Shaded parts
KeyConcepts.Definition: Bottom part gives count of equally-sized pieces in each whole; top gives count colored.
KeyConcepts.Example: 5/8 is five blue out of eight.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole from all pieces
KeyConcepts.Definition: When all b unit parts of one whole are shaded, b/b equals1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fractions above one
KeyConcepts.Definition: Count corresponding sized parts across more than one whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source3/4
WorkedExamples.Question: Source table shows three shaded fourths.
WorkedExamples.Method: Partition each whole into equal-size unit parts and count all shaded parts.
Steps: Each original whole is divided into four equal pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source3/8
WorkedExamples.Question: Last first source table row.
WorkedExamples.Method: Partition each whole into equal-size unit parts and count all shaded parts.
Steps: Eight equal pieces in a2×4 diagram.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source6/4
WorkedExamples.Question: Second source table has two whole rectangles.
WorkedExamples.Method: Partition each whole into equal-size unit parts and count all shaded parts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source7/6
WorkedExamples.Question: Second source table final row.
WorkedExamples.Method: Partition each whole into equal-size unit parts and count all shaded parts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source5/8

WorkedExamples.Method: Partition each whole into equal-size unit parts and count all shaded parts.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Say 6/4 or7/6 cannot be shown by shapes because top bigger than bottom.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original source draws MORE THAN ONE equally sized whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count units across two equally partitioned whole rectangles.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume Part2 game cards have fixed publisher-supplied four fractions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original asks each pair of pupils to CREATE FOUR new matches from eight blank cards.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Introduce technical terms as if required in original first lesson.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original teacher narrative says the formal names are introduced in a later section.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Emphasize top/bottom meaning and delay formal vocabulary.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up shades one, two, three, four fourths.
Matching game includes two rounds and four pupil-authored card pairs.
Whole fractions2/2,3/3,4/4,6/6 all equal1;7/6 is greater than1.
Source image tables inspected, protected Cool-down and Stage D deferred.
